candidates.what: The Clerk's Financial Disclosure pages, which publish the index and the documents
The Committee's filing-deadlines page, on what makes an electronic filing timely
The Committee's memorandum of 30 January 2023 on these reports' due dates
Each electronically filed report's own last line, which the filing system prints as the date the filer digitally signed it
The Committee's Instruction Guide for 2025 filings, which says when an electronically filed report is timely and does not define the index's FilingDate

check: For the 54 reports with no signature line the register can read: ask the Legislative Resource Center in writing what the index date records for a report filed on paper, and record the answer with the date it was given.
holder: The Clerk of the House, on each report it publishes: the filing system prints the date the filer signed it
question: Is the date beside a report the day the member filed it, or the day the Clerk published it?
route: Read the last line of each electronically filed report at disclosures-clerk.house.gov; python tools/check-signed-dates.py does it for every transaction report the register holds, on the sealed bytes, and fails if any was signed on another day than the index gives it.
today: Read at the source on 2026-09-27. On all 409 of the 463 transaction reports in the Clerk's 2025 index whose text the register can read, the date the index gives the report is the date the report's own last line says the filer digitally signed it, checked on bytes whose SHA-256 is the sealed one; on none is it another day, and that includes every report a current Finding rests on. The other 54 carry no signature line the register can read, and for them the question stays open; no Finding rests on any of them. Neither the Clerk's Financial Disclosure pages nor the Committee's 2025 Instruction Guide defines the field; the guide says an electronically filed report is timely when it is filed on or before its due date.
with_it: Every sentence here about a report dated after a deadline rests on the day its filer signed it, not on a day the Clerk published it, so no report here reads as late because it was posted late. The register reads the day of the signature and not its hour.

candidates.what: The Clerk's Financial Disclosure pages
Each document's own header, which prints its Filing Type (or, on an extension request, the Report Type Due), its Filing Year and its Filing Date

check: Read the header of every document in the index, not a sample, at build time, and record what each says of itself; and ask the Legislative Resource Center in writing whether the codes have a published legend.
holder: The Clerk of the House, on each document it publishes: the filing system prints the document's own type in its header
question: What do the Clerk's one-letter form codes mean?
route: Read the header of each document at disclosures-clerk.house.gov; the adapter can record the Filing Type, Filing Year and Filing Date it prints, at build time, for every document it fetches.
today: Read at the source on 2026-09-27. The Clerk's Financial Disclosure pages carry no legend for the codes, so the codes themselves stay uninterpreted. The documents do not need them: each prints its own type in its header. Of a sample read that day, all 24 A documents: 20 say Filing Type: Amendment Report and 4 carry no text; none says Annual. 40 of the 422 O documents: 38 say Filing Type: Annual Report, by a Member, and 2 carry no text. 20 of the 276 X documents: 14 are requests to extend an Original Report and 1 a New Filer Report, and 5 carry no text. A sample describes the documents it read and does not define a code.
with_it: A Signal about any report other than a transaction report can read each document's own Filing Type line and never the index's code, so no row rests on a guess about what a letter means. The guess this row was written to refuse would have been wrong: A is not the annual report.

candidates.what: data/transactions.ndjson, filing_status Amended and Deleted

question: Did the member amend the report afterwards?
route: None needed. The rows are in the sealed build and the filings index carries an amends field that is null on every row today.
today: The register already holds this and does not yet use it: of 7,346 transaction rows, 5 are marked Amended and 2 Deleted by the filer. The signal sets those rows aside and no page follows an amendment back to the report it amends.
with_it: An amendment is the one part of what-followed that the register can see today. A report whose dates a later filing corrects could say so beside the Finding, and a Finding an amendment invalidates could be superseded, which LIMITATIONS 7 already promises and no code yet does.

candidates.what: The Committee on Ethics, which the memorandum names as setting the fee
Its memorandum of 30 January 2023, for what it says about who assesses and records

check: Read what the Committee publishes about late filing fees: its filing-deadlines pages, its annual report to the House, and any list of assessments. Record what exists and what does not, with the date read. Whether such a record is published at all is the first thing to settle.
question: Was the $200 late fee assessed on this report?
route: Unknown. No route this project has established. A record naming a member and a period would not name a Filing ID, so joining it to a report would be an inference, and an inference published against a named person is the defect this project exists to prevent.
today: Nothing. The register holds no row about any fee, on any report, for anyone. It reads the Clerk's filing index and a fee is not in it.
with_it: A report dated after the deadline could say whether the rule's own consequence followed, which is the difference between a register of dates and a register of accountability.

candidates.what: The Committee's filing-deadlines page, which states the waiver standard

check: Read whether the Committee publishes waivers at all, and whether it publishes the ground. Record what the published standard says beyond the four words exceptional circumstances.
question: Was the fee waived, and on what stated ground?
route: Unknown. Same as the assessment: a waiver record would name a member and a period, not a report.
today: Nothing. The Committee's filing-deadlines page says the fee may be waived in exceptional circumstances; what counts as one, and which reports got one, is not in anything the register reads.
with_it: The register could say that a report's fee was waived, on the ground the Committee gave, which is as important to publish as an assessment and points the other way. A waiver is a fact that protects a filer, and a loop closed only on assessments would be a loop closed against people.

candidates.what: The Committee's Summary of Activities for the 118th Congress, its most recent account of its work
5 U.S.C. § 13106(d), which sets the fee and says where it goes

check: Read the 118th Congress Summary of Activities' sections on financial disclosure by eye, or with an extraction that recovers every page, for any count of late fees assessed, waived or paid. If none, the Committee is the one to ask, and the chamber-year count names nobody.
holder: House Committee on Ethics; the Treasury, if the fees are deposited as miscellaneous receipts
question: How many late fees were assessed, waived and collected across the chamber in a year?
route: An annual count, published or answered in writing. A count is not a disclosure about any person and needs no identifier to join.
today: Partly read on 2026-09-27. 5 U.S.C. § 13106(d)(1) sets the $200 fee for a report filed more than 30 days after the later of its due date or the last day of a granted extension, and says the fees "shall be deposited in the miscellaneous receipts of the Treasury"; (d)(2) lets the fee be waived in extraordinary circumstances. A text search of the Committee's 339-page Summary of Activities for the 118th Congress found no mention of a late fee, a filing fee or $200, but the register's extraction recovered about 450 characters a page, less than a page of type holds, so it cannot say the summary is silent. No count of fees has been found anywhere.
with_it: A reader could see whether the rule's consequence operates at all, without a single person being named. Three numbers a year would answer most of what a reader wants and cost no one their privacy, which is why this row is here separately from the two above it.

candidates.what: The Office of Congressional Ethics
The Committee on Ethics

check: Read what the Office of Congressional Ethics publishes: its reports and findings, its quarterly summaries, and the rule under which a Committee extension withholds a report from publication. Read what the Committee publishes when it takes up or disposes of a matter. Record what each actually carries, not what it is reputed to carry.
holder: House Committee on Ethics; the Office of Congressional Ethics
question: Did anyone review this report, and what came of it?
route: Unknown from this project. The Office of Congressional Ethics is a separate body that refers matters to the Committee, and some of what it produces is understood to be published; none of it has been read here.
today: Nothing. The register holds no row about a review of any report, and does not know whether reviews of these reports happen, are recorded, or are published.
with_it: A report could carry the plainest fact of all: that it was looked at, or that no public record says it was. The second sentence is as publishable as the first and the register cannot write either.

candidates.what: The Office of Congressional Conduct's quarterly reports, each with a statistical summary of its Board's actions in the Congress

check: Read the Board Actions table of the latest quarterly report and record what its rows and columns count, and whether any separates financial-disclosure matters.
holder: The Office of Congressional Conduct (formerly the Office of Congressional Ethics), and the House Committee on Ethics
question: How many matters of this kind reached each stage in a year?
route: Read the Board Actions table in each quarterly report at conduct.house.gov, by eye if the text cannot be extracted, and record the counts by stage without the names the reports' own narrative sometimes carries.
today: Read at the source on 2026-09-27. oce.house.gov now redirects to conduct.house.gov: the office is the Office of Congressional Conduct, formerly the Office of Congressional Ethics, and it publishes a report every quarter with a statistical summary of its Board's actions in the Congress, the latest read being the second quarter of 2026. Those are counts for every matter the office reviews. In the report read, the summary is a table the register's text extraction does not recover, so whether it separates financial-disclosure matters from the rest is not something the register can say yet.
with_it: The register could show the shape of the funnel after its own: reports late, matters opened, matters referred, matters disposed. Four numbers a year would let a reader judge the process without judging a person, which is the only judging this project supports.

candidates.what: Federal district court dockets, searched by the statute
5 U.S.C. 13106, for the action the statute provides

check: Read 5 U.S.C. 13106 at its source for what action lies, who may bring it and in what court. Then search the federal dockets by that statute. Record the search, its date and its result, including a result of none, which is a finding.
holder: The United States district courts; the Department of Justice as plaintiff
question: Has the Attorney General ever brought a civil action over one of these filings?
route: Federal dockets. A docket is a public record and machine-readable through the courts' own system and its mirrors; nothing here has been read from either.
today: Nothing. STANDARDS.md S.2 records that the Ethics in Government Act provides penalties for knowingly and willfully failing to file or falsifying a report, and cites 5 U.S.C. 13106; the register reads no court record and holds no row about one.
with_it: The one part of what-follows that happens in open court, where a docket is a primary source anyone can read. A count, or a named case where one exists, with its docket number.

candidates.what: Committee statements on the disposition of a matter

check: Read whether the Committee publishes the fact of a referral, and where. Record what it says and what it does not.
question: Was a matter referred out of the chamber?
today: Nothing. The register does not know whether referrals of this kind are made, recorded, or published.
with_it: The link between the two halves of this list: the chamber's own process and the courts. Without it a court record and a committee record cannot be read as one story even when they are one.

candidates.what: 5 U.S.C. 552, the federal records-request statute, and its definition of agency
5 U.S.C. 551, which that definition refers to
The Rules of the House of Representatives, on the Committee's proceedings

check: Read the Rules of the House on the Committee on Ethics, House Rule XI clause 3, and the Committee's own rules, for what the Committee releases and when.
holder: The statute, and the House's own rules
question: Can a member of the public compel any of this with a records request?
route: Read the statute's own definition of what it applies to.
today: Read at the source on 2026-09-27. 5 U.S.C. § 551(1) defines agency as "each authority of the Government of the United States" but "does not include— (A) the Congress", and § 552(f)(1) uses that definition for the records-request statute. So in the statute's own words a records request does not reach the Congress; the register reads that as reaching the House, its Clerk and its Committee on Ethics, and has not read a court's holding on it. What the Committee releases of its own accord is a question for the House's rules, which have not been read here yet.
with_it: Every row above that says unknown stays a request the holder may answer or decline, never one a reader can compel; the page can say so plainly, and the chamber-year counts become the asks that cost nobody anything.

check: Read the House rule that governs the confidentiality of the Committee's proceedings, and record what it protects and why, in the rule's own words rather than this project's.
question: What is in the Committee's own file on a matter?
route: None sought. This row exists so the list cannot be read as asking for everything.
today: Nothing, and this is the one row on this list the register does not argue should change.
with_it: Nothing the register should publish. A file that contains an unproven allegation against a person, and the person's answer to it, is the kind of record whose confidentiality protects exactly the reader this project is built for: the one who has not done anything and should not have to prove it. The same confidentiality means nobody outside can tell whether a founded complaint was acted on. Both are true, and the second does not cancel the first.

check: Settle every other row on this page first. This one is written last, from what they found, and never before.
holder: The House, in its rules; the Congress, in statute
question: If none of it is obtainable, what would have to change?
route: Not a route. A statement, once the rows above are settled, of which of them no existing route reaches.
today: The register asks for nothing and proposes nothing. This row records the shape of the gap, not a demand.
with_it: A reader could see which part of this list is a records problem and which part is a rules problem. They are different problems and conflating them is how a register turns into a campaign, which this one does not do.
